preamble: The elision of [ð] is the final stage of dental lenition. In Romance, an intervocalic stop first weakens to [ð] and then disappears, as in Old French (12th century) and in modern Spanish -ado participles. In North Germanic, Old Norse ð was lost in Norwegian and Faroese and is often dropped in Danish.

examples.note: Elision of intervocalic [ð] is most advanced in the -ado participle ending; widespread in Peninsular and many American varieties.
Gallo-Romance [ð] from intervocalic Latin t/d was lost around 1100.
The spelling keeps d, but Old Norse ð is silent.
ð is silent; a hiatus glide [v] or [j] fills the gap before /ʊ, ɪ/.
Variant pronunciation without the soft d.

sources: Molina Martos, I. & Paredes García, F. (2015). Sociolingüística de la elisión de la dental -/d/- en Madrid (Distrito de Salamanca). Cuadernos de Lingüística de El Colegio de México. https://revistas.colmex.mx/Record/oai:oai.cuadernoslinguistica.colmex.mx:article-15
